newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA RAND/BONDS CLOSING REPORT.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA RAND/BONDS CLOSING REPORT.

text.p: A barrage of dollar demand brought the rand's two-day rally to an abrupt halt on Wednesday, forcing it to retrace 450 basis points from its strongest level.
It settled at 4.6575/6625 against the dollar at the 1400 GMT finish compared with 4.6360/6410 overnight.

The currency began the day on a positive footing, scurrying to a day's strongest level of 4.6200 bid where it ran into a large local import order as well as strong demand for dollars from offshore, dealers said.
That demand carried it steadily to a morning's worst level of 4.6640 bid.

Dealers said the currency's woes were compounded by a report released by stockbroking firm PLJ van Rensburg in which economist Vic de Klerk predicted that an International Monetary Fund loan for South Africa was inevitable by the end of February.
De Klerk said the country would be forced to draw down on its IMF quota in order to meet its foreign exchange obligations.
Under IMF rules, South Africa would be able to draw up to 100 percent of its IMF quota -- or some $2 billion -- for use as a standby or extended fund facility.
A finance department spokeswoman reiterated an earlier government statement that the country had no plans to seek an IMF loan in the near-term.
Dealers said the release of worse-than-expected consumer inflation data also brought pressure to bear on the currency.
The CPI data, which rose 1.0 percent month-on-month and 9.1 percent year-on-year, was 0.4 percentage points above a Reuters consensus forecast of an 8.8 percent rise.
Dealers said that while the market had been expecting a weak number, some players had been spooked by the fact that the data was above the 9.0 percent mark.
"The fact that it was was over the figure shook some of the boys a bit," one trader said.
Dealers said were loathe to predict the rand's next move after Wednesday's volatility, preferring only to forecast that it would weaken further on Thursday.

Against the crosses, the rand sank to a new low against sterling of 7.8398 before recovering to 7.8144/8274 at the finish from 7.7585/7715 on Tuesday. It also eased against the German mark to 0.3210/3214 from 0.3237/3242 overnight.
The bond market was led from start to finish by the rand's movement in largely thin volume trade, with the CPI data providing a bump along the way, dealers said.
The key R150 was pegged at a 15.955 percent yield from 15.865 percent overnight before moving to the key 16 percent level in after-hours trade.
"The rand's drop was the cause of it. The CPI was negative, but it was basically already discounted in the market," one trader said.
Dealers said another factor weighing on sentiment had been a rise in the money market shortage which reminded traders of the continuing liquidity squeeze at the short-end of the market.
"The market has tended to overlook the serious squeeze on the short-end over the last two days...the bullishness we have seen cannot be justified by the short-end pressure," another trader said.
The Reserve Bank indicated the daily shortage higher at 9.697 billion on Tuesday compared with 9.064 billion rand on Monday.
Banks quoted their three-month NCD rates unchanged at between 16.95 percent and 17.00 percent offered, while the 90-day BA rate was also unmoved at between 16.30 and 16.60 percent.
Bond traders said direction on Thursday would be dictated by where the rand went next.

The Bond Exchange said foreigners sold a net 48.43 million rand worth of South African bonds on Tuesday after buying 123.88 million rand worth on Monday, while nominal cumulative volumes fell to 3.73 billion rand from 4.87 billion rand on Monday.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482 1003
